intro: Searching for a medical accountant near you usually means your money has become more complicated than a standard tax return can handle — NHS pension figures, locum work, a private clinic or a partnership share. You want someone local who deals with doctors and healthcare professionals as a matter of routine. We can introduce you to a UK accountant suited to that kind of work, and they will quote you directly.
need_heading: What people searching for a medical accountant usually need
need_lead: The situations behind this search tend to involve income and pension questions that go well beyond a straightforward salary.

You work as a locum and your income arrives from several different sources through the year.

context_heading: What to understand about medical accountants
context: In the UK, the word "accountant" on its own is not a protected title, so anyone can call themselves one. Titles such as Chartered Accountant (ICAEW, ICAS or Chartered Accountants Ireland), Chartered Certified Accountant (ACCA) and Chartered Management Accountant (CIMA) are protected, and members are bound by their body's ethics, training and complaints rules. Only registered auditors can sign statutory audit reports.

Every practice offering accountancy services must also be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, either by a professional body or by HMRC. It is reasonable to ask which body supervises a firm, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance, and how complaints are handled. iComply is not regulated and does not give professional advice — we simply make the introduction.

tell: Say whether you are a GP, hospital doctor, consultant, locum or another healthcare professional, so the right kind of accountant is suggested.
Describe your income sources, including NHS work, locum shifts, private practice or a partnership share.
Mention any NHS pension annual allowance concerns you already have, even if they are only at the stage of a warning letter.
Say whether you need help with partnership or practice accounts as well as your personal tax return.
Note where you are based and how far you are willing to travel, since you searched for someone near you.
Mention any deadlines or changes coming up, such as a new partnership or a change in your working pattern.
questions: Do you deal with NHS pension annual allowance issues for doctors as part of your regular work?
How do you handle locum income spread across several sources in one tax year?
Are you a member of AISMA, the Association of Independent Specialist Medical Accountants?
Which body supervises your practice for anti-money-laundering purposes?

Can you explain how private practice and NHS income are kept separate in my accounts?

faqs.q: Why would a doctor need a medical accountant rather than a general one?
faqs.a: Medical accountants work with doctors and healthcare professionals on NHS pensions, locum income, private practice and partnership accounts. Those areas come up constantly in medical careers, so a specialist is more likely to spot the issues early.

faqs.q: What is AISMA and why does it matter?
faqs.a: AISMA is the Association of Independent Specialist Medical Accountants. It is worth asking whether a firm is a member, as it signals a focus on medical work — but check the firm's own credentials too.

faqs.q: How can I judge an accountant when I am searching near me?
faqs.a: Ask about their protected titles and which body supervises them, and whether they handle NHS pensions and locum income regularly. A local firm you can meet face to face may suit you, but the specialist knowledge matters most.

faqs.q: Does iComply provide the accountancy service itself?
faqs.a: No. iComply is a free introduction service — you tell us what you need and we introduce you to a suitable UK professional, who quotes you directly. We are not regulated and do not give professional advice.

extra_heading: Choosing between the medical accountants you find nearby
extra: A search for a medical accountant near me often comes from someone who wants to sit down with their accountant in person, or at least know they are on the same patch. That is a reasonable instinct, but proximity alone tells you nothing about whether a firm actually handles NHS pensions, locum income and practice accounts. Use the location to build a shortlist, then judge each firm on what they do rather than where they are.

When you compare, ask the same questions of each firm and note how clearly they answer. A firm that works with doctors routinely should be able to talk you through how the NHS pension annual allowance is assessed, how locum income from several sources is pulled together, and how partnership accounts differ from a salaried post. If the answers sound vague, that is useful information too.

It also helps to think about how you like to work. Some people want to hand over a shoebox of paperwork and meet once a year; others want to be able to ring with a question mid-year. Ask how the firm prefers to communicate, whether you would deal with the same person each time, and what they need from you to get started. The right fit is about more than the postcode.

extra_faqs.q: Is a medical accountant near me necessarily better than one further away?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Being local can make meetings easier and may mean familiarity with your area, but the deciding factor should be whether the firm regularly handles NHS pensions, locum income and practice accounts. Plenty of people work happily with an accountant they mostly deal with by phone and email.

extra_faqs.q: What should I bring to a first meeting with a medical accountant?
extra_faqs.a: Bring anything that shows your income and pension position: recent tax returns, payslips or locum statements, partnership accounts if you have them, and any letters about your NHS pension. A short note of what you want help with saves time. The accountant can then tell you what else they need and quote you directly.
